2. Complainant-opposite Party No.1 made a complaint before, the court of Magistrate, Tangail against accused petitioners alleging, inter alia, that they in collusion with each other created a forged order purported to be made by then Munsif, 3rd Court, Tangail in Miscellaneous Case No.337 of 1973 under section 143A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, shortly the Act, for correction of the record of right in respect of the case land, that subsequently the petitioners filed the said forged order before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) Mirzapur for correcting the record of rights in their favour, that pursuant thereto, the Assistant Commissioner (Land) issued notice upon the complainant who on enquiry ascertained that petitioners filed a forged copy of the order of the learned Munsif and thereupon filed an application before the Assistant Commissioner (Land) for attaching the said forged order of the learned Munsif for drawing up a proceeding under section 476 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, that the Assistant Commissioner (Land) refused to make any complaint and directed the complainant to file case against the accused and accordingly, complaint was made. 

 8. Now the question is a Revenue Officer, in the instant case Assistant Commissioner (Land), dealing with a Mutation proceeding is a Revenue Court within the meaning of sub-section (1) of section 195 of the Code of Criminal Procedure shortly the Code. In the Code, no definition of the "Revenue Court" has been given. Since there is no definition of Revenue Court in the Code, let us examine other Laws as to the meaning of the term 'Revenue Court. In the Tenancy Law i.e. the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, there is no definition of Revenue Court." The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act only speaks of "Revenue Officer" includes "any officer whom the government may appoint to discharge all or any of the functions of a Revenue officer under this Act or any rules made thereunder". Chapter XVII of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and Chapter VI of the Tenancy Rules 1954 provide the procedure of preparation of the records of rights by the Revenue officer. Sub- section 9(a) of section 3 of the General Clauses Act defines the term "Chief Revenue Officer" means the National Board of Revenue constituted under the National Board of Revenue Order 1972, (president's Order 76 of 1972). Since there is no definition of "Revenue Court" in the Code of Criminal Procedure, the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the General Clauses Act let us examine the meaning of the term "Court." Section 6 of the Code describes classes of criminal Courts, namely: 

 12. As pointed out earlier, the term revenue court has not been defined in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The said .Act only speaks of Revenue Officer. A Revenue Officer initiates a Mutation Proceeding in exercise of powers under section 143 of the State Acquisition .and Tenancy Act 1950 and the Rules framed thereunder. Section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, provides: 

 For carrying out purposes of the Act, the Government promulgated the Tenancy Rules 1954 in exercise of powers conferred under section 152 of the Act. In the said Rules, Rules 22 and 23 provide the procedures and the manner in which the record of rights referred to In section 143 shall be maintained. The relevant portions of Rules 22 and 23 are reproduced below- 

 13. These Rules clearly provide that when Tahsilder primarily responsible for. report to the Revenue Officer apparently makes clerical mistake in record-of-rights, changes of ownership, etc., the Revenue Officer shall direct correction of such clerical mistakes and making such inquiries as he "may consider necessary direct excision of the fraudulent entry and his act being a ministerial act shall not be open to appeal. A Revenue Officer holding an inquiry in a mutation proceeding, in the premises, does not become a court as he does not really adjudicate a right and he does not give a decision which is binding on the parties. He merely corrects apparent clerical mistakes in the record-of-rights and directs correction of such clerical mistakes. If he is vested with necessary powers, incorporates necessary changes in the record-of-rights mutating the names when mutation is asked for as a result of inheritance on the report of Tahsilder under Rule 22 and also when mutation is asked for as a result of transfer, his acts being ministerial acts, shall not be open to appeal as provided in Rule 23 sub-rule (4) of the Tenancy Rules, 1954. He certainly exercises no judicial function. The functions are much more in the nature of a fiscal enquiry for the purpose of ascertaining which of the several claimants for the occupation of certain denominations of immovable property may be put into occupation of it with greater confidence than the revenue for which will be paid. Inquiry in mutation proceedings, therefore, being a fiscal inquiry conducted by agents of the State, for their own purposes, it could by no means be described as judicial proceeding. Therefore, a Revenue Officer when dealing with a mutation proceedings does not constitute a "Revenue Court" within the wider meaning of section 195(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 "We are in full agreement with the view expressed in the aforesaid decisions. We are, therefore, of the opinion that a Revenue Officer dealing with a mutation proceeding under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and Rules framed thereunder does not constitute a court. Since we have found that a Revenue Officer acting under Rule 23 of the Tenancy Rules is not a Court, it is needless for us to dilate on the question whether he is a civil, criminal or Revenue Court." 

 "We respectfully disagree with the above views of the Division Bench which held that Revenue Officer doing mutation matter is not a Revenue Court. Tenancy Rules 30 and 31 deal with preparation of record-of-rights and Tenancy Rules 20-24 deal with correction of records of right by way of Mutation. Both the matters are dealt with by the Revenue Officers and regarding Mutation matter there is a provision for review to the Revenue Officer. Weare of the view that the principle applicable to preparation of record of right also be applicable to the mutation of name in the record of rights inasmuch as both relate to preparation, modification, addition or alteration of record of rights. Relying upon the principles as laid down by the Appellate Division in above decision reported in BCR 1987 (AD) 152, we hold that the Revenue Officer dealing in Mutation of the name in the record of rights is also a Revenue Court. As we are holding this view relying upon the above decision of the Appellate Division, we need not refer this matter to a Full Bench for our disagreement with another Division Bench." 

 16. The said decision of the Division Bench in the case of Ajit Kumar Sarker was mainly based upon the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Nur Ahmed (Supra) holding that since the Appellate Division has settled the point, the learned Judge felt it not necessary to refer the matter to a Full Bench for settling the point. Let us now examine the case of Nur Ahmed (Supra) and if the decision of the Appellate Division is exactly on the point, then certainly the said decision is binding on us and we are bound to follow that decision. In the Appellate Division's case, a complaint was lodged by a care-taker of Kodam Mobarak and Adam Rasul Waqf Estate before the Metropolitan Magistrate, Chittagong to the effect that he received a notice from the Objection Officer of Settlement Department and pursuant thereto, on query came to learn that accused had filed an objection case alleging that he has purchased the land in dispute and filed the deed before the objection officer, which was a forged deed. The complainant brought to the notice of the Objection Officer about the said forgery whereupon the Objection Officer seized the kabala. Accordingly, the learned Magistrate issued process upon the accused persons under sections 467/468/109 of the Penal Code. In the said case the Appellate Division upon consideration of Rules 30, 31 and 39 of the Tenancy Rules, 1954 held that: 

 "Reading the provisions of Rules 30 and 39 ,of the Tenancy Rules 1954, there could be no difficulty in holding that Mr Golam Mostafa, the Objection Officer was functioning as a Revenue Court while the alleged document was placed before him in connection with proceeding under Rule 30 of the said Tenancy Rules and as such, section 195(c) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is clearly attracted which puts an embargo on taking cognizance of the alleged offence under sections 467 and 468 of the Penal Code in the absence of a complaint from the court concerned". 

 17. In the Appellate Division's case the issue was whether an Objection Officer having power of an Assistant Settlement Officer in deciding Objection Petition is a Revenue Court or not. The Appellate Division upon consideration of Rules 30, 31 and 39 of the Tenancy Rules 1954 held that a Revenue Officer having additional powers of Settlement Officer while hearing objection case shall have all powers exercisable by a civil court in a trial of suits under Civil Procedure Code and decides ownership or possession of land or of any interest in land and therefore, the objection officer is functioning as a "Revenue Court". These Rules were framed for carrying out the purpose and the manner in which revision of the record-of-rights can be prepared under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Section 144 provides: 

 These rules are included in chapter VII of the Tenancy Rules 1954 under the heading "Revision of record of rights under section 144 of the Act." This chapter deals with the particulars to be recorded at the stages of the work, procedure of work up to attestation, publication of draft record of rights, objection, appeal, publication of final records, certificate of final publication, presumption as to correctness of record of rights, powers of Revenue Officers, etc. while revising the record-of-rights under section 144 of the Act. After such revision of the record-of-rights at the instance of the Government of any district, part of a district or local area by the Revenue Officer appointed for the purpose who shall have either with or without the additional designation of "Settlement Officer", or "Assistant Settlement Officer", such Revenue Officer shall publish a draft record-of-rights by placing it for public inspection at such convenient place as he may determine and a proclamation be published informing the tenants/maliks for filing objections. After hearing the objections, if any, he shall proceed to frame the final record-of-rights. Similarly, in case of an appeal, the Appellate Officer shall give the parties an opportunity of being heard and shall record in the proceedings an abstract of the reasons for his decision. The provisions of Act and the Rules clearly show that the revision of the record-of-rights made under section 144 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act has' presumptive value, but any order of mutation of the record made under section 143 of the Act has no such presumptive value. A Revenue Officer appointed with the power of Settlement Officer shall have all powers exercisable by a Civil Court in the trial of suits under the Code of Civil Procedure. These Rules and the rules framed by the Governor in Council of Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 are closely akin Rule 36 of the Tenancy Rules 1954 is similar to Rule 41 of the Bengal Rules. Similarly, Rules 39 and 40 are equivalent to Rules 44 and 45 of Bengal Rules. The Bengal Government Rules were framed for carrying out the purpose of chapter X of the Bengal Tenancy Act. It is settled that the record of rights prepared in chapter I of the Bengal Tenancy Act i.e. under sections 101-104 of the Bengal Tenancy Act have the presumptive value as in section 144 of the Act but such presumption is not available in section 143 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In the Appellate Division's case no argument was made as to whether a Revenue Officer dealing with Mutation proceeding is a Revenue Court or not and naturally the Appellate Division has not decided the said issue. We are, therefore, of the opinion that the decision of the Appellate Division in the case of Nur Ahmed is quite distinguishable from the facts of the case of Idris Ali (38 DLR 270) and the case of Ajit Kumar Sarkar (44 DLR 533). The Appellate Division case was decided upon consideration of the Rules contained in Chapter VII and VIII of the Tenancy Rules 1954 which were framed in exercise of section 152(2)(2b) of the Act, for carrying out the purposes for all or any of the provisions of section 144 of the Act which the facts in the case of Idris Ali (Supra) and that of Ajit Kumar Sarkar(Supra) are similar to the present case, which relate to mutation proceedings under section 143 of the Act and Chapter VI of the Tenancy Rules 1954 framed in exercise of section 152 (2)(2a) of the Act. In the premises aforesaid, we are in respectful agreement with the views taken by the Division of the High Court Division in the case of Idris Ali (Supra). For the reasons discussed above and the provisions of law quoted herein before, with due respect to the learned Judges of the High Court Division, we are unable to endorse the views taken by them in the case of Ajit Kumar Sarkar (Supra). 

 20. It has been pointed out earlier that the High Court Division, in the case of Ajit Kumar Sarker and others (Supra) based its decision relying upon the case of the Appellate Division, the facts of which are quite distinguishable from the case of the case reported in the case of Noor Ahmed and the High Court Division without examining the relevant provisions of law i.e. section 143 of the Act and chapter VI of the Tenancy Rules 1954, held that a "Revenue Officer" dealing with mutation proceeding is a "Revenue Court." Therefore, we are unable to approve the views taken in that case and consequently, we are of the opinion that the matter need not be referred for decision to a larger Bench since there is earlier decision of a Division bench over the said issue, with whom we are in full agreement. Accordingly, we approve the decision of the Division Bench in the case of Idris Ali. Our view is that a Revenue Officer when dealing with a Mutation Proceeding does not constitute a Revenue Court within the meaning of section 195(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure and therefore, a Criminal Court can take cognizance of any offence described in sections 463 and 471, 475 and 476 of the Penal Code on the basis of complaint filed by any aggrieved party when such offence is alleged to have been committed by a party to any Mutation proceeding in respect of a document produced or given in evidence in such proceeding. Accordingly, we find no substance in the submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioners.
